activity: to measure the speed of a rolling ball from distance and time and draw a distance-time graph
story:
Isabella had enrolled in the after-school science club mostly because her friend Marisol had, but now the club's project was due Monday and she was stuck. The assignment was to roll a ball down the hallway, measure its distance every second, and draw a distance-time graph from the numbers. The graph was supposed to show the ball slowing down as it rolled across the carpet. Hers showed something strange.

"Watch," she said to Marisol, who had come over Sunday afternoon. Isabella crouched at the end of the hallway with a stopwatch and a marble. "I roll it, I call the seconds, you write the distance." She flicked the marble. It zipped along the wood floor, hit the rug by the bathroom door, wobbled, and stopped. Every time she tried it, the marble died in the same spot.

They collected the numbers at the kitchen table. Isabella drew the axes, marked time across the bottom and distance up the side, and plotted each point. From two seconds to four seconds, the points sat at exactly the same height: thirty centimeters, thirty centimeters, thirty centimeters. She connected them with a straight, level stretch of line.

"That part looks broken," Marisol said, poking the flat section. "The rest of your line climbs, then it just goes sideways."

Isabella looked at the stopwatch log, then down the hall at the marble still sitting on the rug. It hadn't moved between those seconds at all. The line wasn't broken. "It's not climbing because the ball isn't going anywhere," she said. "A flat line means the ball stopped." She picked up the marble and rolled it again, slower, watching the rug. The marble's own fuzz of dust clung to the carpet fibers, and it sank in and stayed. That was it, not her timing, not her measurements.

For Monday's graph she traced the flat stretch with a red pencil and wrote "ball stuck on rug" above it in small letters. Then she rolled the marble one more time down the hall, but this time she lifted the corner of the rug and let it fly onto the bare wood.

"Now watch it climb," she said.

activity: to cook rice, a curry and flatbread so they are all ready at the same time
story:
The community kitchen on Harlow Street smelled like onions and warm spice, and Lucy had been assigned to the whole meal, not just one dish. Rice, curry, flatbread, all finished at the same time, so the plates went out hot. The teacher, Ms. Okafor, called this "real cooking," and Lucy had been proud of the word until she stood in front of three burners and realized she had no idea how to make three things land together.

She started with the rice, since it looked like the slowest. Wash, water, pot, lid, flame. Then she mixed curry paste and coconut milk in a second pot and set it on low. The flatbread dough she would roll and cook last, in a dry pan, quick as anything. On the wall above the stoves hung a faded map of the river delta where Ms. Okafor had grown up, and the label on it read "estuary," the wide mouth where the river met the sea. Lucy traced it with her eyes while she stirred and wondered whether food from a place like that tasted like both river and salt.

Beside her, a boy named Devon kept lifting the lid off his pot of rice. Peek, stir, lid. Peek again. "I just want to see if it's working," he said, a little embarrassed.

"Rice isn't much to look at," Lucy said, but she was thinking harder than that. When the class did a trial run the week before, Devon's rice had come out crunchy in the middle while everyone else's was soft, and he had shrugged and blamed the bag. Lucy hadn't shrugged. She kept turning the question over. Same rice, same water, same stove. The only thing different she could remember was Devon, hovering and lifting, again and again. Could she deduce the cause from that? If the difference wasn't the rice or the pot, it had to be something Devon did, and the one thing he did more than anyone was open the lid.

She didn't say any of this out loud. Instead she made a plan for her own pot, a small test. She would not lift the lid at all, not once, from the moment it started steaming until the timer rang. Her curry needed stirring, and the flatbread needed her full attention with the rolling pin, so her hands were busy anyway. The hardest part was her own worry, the itch to check. She pressed the lid down a little firmer, like sealing a promise.

While the bread bubbled on the dry pan, she counted backward from the clock to figure out timing. Curry off the heat now, bread in thirty-second rounds, rice resting with the flame off and the lid still on. When everything was down to the last minute, she finally lifted her lid. Steam rolled out in one white cloud, and underneath, the grains stood plump and separate and fully cooked, all the way through.

Devon leaned over and looked at her pot, then at his own, which he had peeked at four more times. "Yours didn't crunch," he said.

"Don't lift the lid while it simmers," Lucy said. "Every peek lets the steam out, and then the rice can end up undercooked."

Devon squinted at his pot as if it had betrayed him personally. "So I did this to myself."

"Try one with the lid staying shut," Lucy said. "I'll roll you a flatbread while you wait."

He refilled his pot, set the lid on carefully, and then sat on his hands.

activity: to chop an onion safely with the claw grip and make a pasta sauce from scratch
story:
Sara curled her fingers into a claw above the onion, knuckles forward, exactly the way the chef's poster showed, and brought the knife down in slow, parallel cuts. The kitchen of Uncle Ray's restaurant smelled of garlic and scorched tomato from the batch before hers, and her eyes were already stinging. "Keep your fingertips under," said Marcus, the dishwasher's son, who wanted to be a line cook someday and never let anyone forget it. "You slice a thumb in here, my dad says you mop the floor for a week." Sara adjusted her grip and wondered whether the cooks who never cried at onions had simply stopped noticing, or whether their knives were sharper than this one.

Her task was real: the Saturday sauce. Uncle Ray had put two pounds of pasta on to boil for the dinner rush and told her the sauce had to cling, not slide, or the plates would look like soup. She crushed the canned tomatoes with her hands, which felt satisfyingly against the rules, and added her chopped onion to the hissing oil. It smelled like a real kitchen, like the one she imagined when she wrote stories, where the narrator always knew what everyone was tasting.

The sauce simmered, but when she dragged a spoon through it, the tomato part stayed thin and watery, and a slick of oil floated beside it, refusing to join. She tasted it and frowned. Something was wrong, and she could not see what. She checked the heat, lowered it, tasted again. Thin, still thin. She began to wonder whether the problem was not what she had added but something she had left out, some invisible ingredient the recipe assumed.

Then Marcus called from the sink, where he was about to dump the giant pot of cloudy pasta water down the drain. "Wait," Sara said, hurrying over. The water was milky white, not clear, and she dipped a finger in and rubbed her fingertips together. Slick. She remembered the water turning that way as the pasta cooked, and she thought, this water changed while the pasta was in it. "The pasta releases starch into the water," she said slowly, half asking herself. She ladled out a cupful before Marcus could tip the rest away. "A splash of this might help a sauce thicken and cling to the pasta. That's what cloudy means here."

She stirred the splash into her sauce and watched. Within a minute the spoon left a clean trail, and when she lifted it, the sauce hung on, thick and glossy, the oil no longer swimming apart from the tomato. She tasted it and grinned at Marcus, who leaned over her shoulder and sniffed. "Okay, I confess, I thought you were ruining it," he said. She dipped two clean spoons into the pot and handed him one. "Try it before the dinner rush does."

activity: to play a piece with dynamics and tempo changes in a band or on the piano
story:
Jade had one week to get the duet right before the family reunion at Grandma's house, and the piano was not helping. Grandma's old upright had a sticky E key and a bench that wobbled, but it was the only piano for miles, so Jade spread her music on the rack and practiced until her fingers ached. Her cousin Marco was supposed to play clarinet with her, and he had texted that morning: "Question. On measure 32 there's 'rit.' and on measure 48 there's 'accel.' What do those even do? Also why does your grandma only have saltine crackers?"

Jade wrote back a letter, because Grandma's internet only worked in the kitchen and Jade refused to drag the whole music binder in there. "Dear Marco," she wrote. "Grandma is frugal, that's why the crackers. Stop eating the crackers and practice. For the other thing, I'm working on it." She was not entirely working on it. She had played the piece twenty times, and every time something strange happened at measure 32, like the song lost its balance, and she could not see why. The notes were right. The counting was right. Something invisible was hiding in the music, and she wanted to find it more than she wanted lunch.

She found the first clue by accident. When she slowed way down on purpose at measure 32, just to read a tricky fingering, the weird feeling vanished. The music suddenly made sense, like it wanted to ease off there. That gave her an idea she could test. She played the whole piece again and slowed gradually at the word "rit.," a little more with every beat, then sped back up gradually after it. It worked. At "accel." she did the opposite, pressing faster by small degrees, and the ending swept up like a wave. She jumped off the bench and shouted to Grandma in the kitchen, "It's a secret message in the sheet music!"

The second clue came from an old recording Grandma had of the piece. Jade played it three times, tapping her foot against the wobbly bench, and sure enough, the pianist on the recording slowed at exactly measure 32 and sped up near the end. When Marco video-called that evening, clarinet in hand, Jade was ready. "Watch me," she said, "and do what my hands do." They started together, and at measure 32 they both stretched the beat out, then pushed it forward again at the end, and they finished at the exact same moment. Marco lifted his clarinet overhead like a trophy.

"So that's it," Marco said, grinning through the screen. "Ritardando means gradually slowing down, and accelerando means the opposite." Jade nodded and flipped the page. "Same time tomorrow. Grandma says she'll delegate snack duty to Aunt Renee, so there might be actual food."

"Also," Marco added, "I'm basically a herbivore, so tell Aunt Renee I want the veggie tray." Jade laughed, set her hands on the keys, and counted them in: "One, two, ready, play."

activity: to explain how nicotine causes addiction in the brain's reward pathway
story:
Jaxon stood at the kitchen counter with his laptop open and a pile of index cards beside the fruit bowl. Tomorrow he had to stand up in health class and explain how nicotine hooks the brain, and every time he tried to say it out loud, the words tangled like earbuds in a pocket. His mother stirred soup at the stove, and the window above the sink held the last gray light of the afternoon.

"Explain it to me," his mother said, tasting from the wooden spoon. "I'm your practice audience."

He took a breath. "Okay. There's this part of the brain called the reward pathway. It's what makes you feel good when you eat a good meal or win a game. Nicotine tricks it. It gets into the brain and pushes that pathway to release dopamine, which is a chemical that signals, hey, that was great, do it again."

"And that's the trap," his mother said.

"Right, because the feeling fades fast, so the brain keeps asking for more." He shuffled his cards, then stopped, because the cards weren't the problem. He remembered Tuesday's class, how Mr. Reyes had put a number on the board without a single comment, just the number, and let the room sit with it. Nearly 9 out of 10 adults who smoke cigarettes daily first tried smoking by age 18. Jaxon had copied it down slowly, and around him kids had stopped whispering. That was the fact he wanted to end with, but he wasn't sure yet how to make it land. He decided to test it, the way he tested things, on his little sister.

Nia was at the table drawing cats with brown whiskers. He sat down across from her. "Nia, quick question. If nine out of ten grown-ups who smoke every day, almost all of them, first tried it by age eighteen, what does that tell you?"

She looked up, pencil paused. "That they started when they were kids. Like, my age almost."

"Exactly like your age almost." He turned back toward the stove, feeling something click into place, quiet and certain. It wasn't a random fact to stick on the last slide. It was the whole point. The brain builds its want early, and nine out of ten times it starts before anyone is old enough to know better.

That evening, after the dishes, he narrated the presentation twice in his room, start to finish, pacing between the bed and the closet. It had become a small ritual: cards down, lights low, speaking to the desk lamp as if it were the class. On the second run he didn't stumble once. He finished with the number, held up both hands with nine fingers spread, and said, "Nine out of ten. Before eighteen." Then he picked up his cards, squared their edges, and set them by the door for morning.

activity: to look at onion skin cells under a microscope and label the cell wall, membrane and nucleus
story:
Nevaeh had the kitchen table to herself for exactly one hour, because that was the deal. Her brother Dex, who was nine and had negotiated hard, wanted the microscope for his "mystery puddle water" after dinner, and Mom had said one hour each, no appeals.

The onion sat on the cutting board like a small, smelly prisoner. Nevaeh's assignment said she had to find the cells in a piece of onion skin, draw them, and label the cell wall, the membrane, and the nucleus. The assignment did not say how to do any of that, which she assumed was part of the challenge. She peeled a paper-thin layer off the inside of an onion ring, laid it on the slide, dropped on a coverslip, and pressed her eye to the lens.

She saw purple. Then she saw purple swirls, like turbulent water in a tiny river, and then she saw nothing but her own eyelashes. She spun the focus knob back and forth. Nothing. She checked the slide. Still there. She checked the onion. Still an onion. The cells, according to the diagram in her book, should look like neat little bricks in a wall, and there was not one brick anywhere in the purple storm.

Dex wandered in with his puddle water in a jelly jar. "My turn yet?"

"Forty-five more minutes."

"Mrs. Tanuya lets us look at parameciums in science. She says you have to find them on the little lens first, the low power one, and then switch to the big ones after." He shrugged. "I don't know why. It's just the rule."

Nevaeh looked at the microscope. There were three lenses on the rotating nosepiece, and she had, without thinking, started with the longest one, the biggest, the one that seemed like it ought to show the most. She rotated to the shortest lens, the lowest power, and pressed her eye to the glass. Bricks. Rows and rows of pale, wobbly bricks, like a wall someone had built while tired. She focused slowly, and the edges sharpened, and there in each brick sat a small dark dot, round and stubborn. The nucleus. The wall was the brick edge itself, and the membrane hugged it from the inside, thin as a rumor.

"Ha," she said.

"You found them?"

"Found them, drew them, labeled them." She was already sketching fast, because a rule discovered at minute forty of a forty-five minute turn is a rule discovered barely in time. Dex hovered behind her, holding his jelly jar up to the window light.

"Can I do the low-power thing on my puddle?"

"You can do the whole thing on your puddle." She slid the microscope across the table to him. "Start with the smallest lens."

"Which one's that?"

"The one closest to the slide," Nevaeh said, "that looks like it can't possibly be useful."

activity: to run an eight-hundred-metre race pacing the first lap so there is energy for the second
story:
Alexandre had finished dead last in the first eight-hundred-metre time trial, and he knew exactly why: he had sprinted the first lap as if it were the only lap. By the final straight his legs felt like they belonged to someone else, someone slower, and three boys had passed him one after another while he watched them go. That night he wrote an email to his friend Priya, who missed practice because her family had gone to visit her grandmother.

"You will laugh," he typed. "Coach timed us, and I ran my first lap ten seconds faster than my second. TEN. I was the early leader for about ninety glorious seconds, and then I became a statue with legs. Dylan passed me. Then Marcus. Then a kid I have never spoken to in my life, who said 'good race' in a pity voice. Tomorrow I am going to try something: run the first lap slower on purpose, a pace I can actually hold, and see what happens to the second lap. If this fails too, I am taking up chess."

Priya's reply came the next morning, printed out and folded into his shoe, which was her idea of a mailbox. "Chess is a sport for people who fade on the final straight," she wrote. "But modify your plan slightly: don't run the first lap slow like you're strolling through a lush garden. Run it even. Save the speed. Also, your shoe-mail system needs work, my note smells like your gym bag."

At practice, the track was bright after rain, and Coach Russell waved them to the line. Alexandre hung back when the gun went off, letting Dylan and Marcus charge ahead. His legs begged him to chase them, but he counted his steps and kept the pace steady, even, holding it the way Priya had said. Down the first back straight Dylan was five metres up and pulling away, and Alexandre felt the old pull to follow. He let Dylan go.

Then the second lap began, and the race turned inside out. Dylan's shoulders dropped, his stride shortened, and he slowed sharply, as if the first lap had cost him something invisible that was now gone. Alexandre came past him on the final bend, and Marcus too, whose early lead had evaporated the same way. Alexandre crossed the line second, gasping but upright, and Priya's note was still crumpled in his shoe.

"Good race," Dylan panted, leaning on his knees, and this time it didn't sound like pity at all. Alexandre grinned and pulled the soggy paper from his shoe, holding it up like a medal.

story:
The pool parking lot had been turned into a squiggly eight-hundred-metre loop with orange cones, and Beatrice stood at the start line in her flip-flops, switching to running shoes with the speed of a firefighter answering a bell. Today was the Summer Splash Classic, and today, she told herself, she would not die on the second lap.

Last year she had died on the second lap. The memory invaded her mind every time she smelled chlorine: her at the front, sprinting like a maniac on lap one, then her legs turning to wet noodles while Priya Chandra floated past her looking fresh as a lemonade stand. Priya had won the giant plastic trophy, a gold cup the size of a birdbath, and had carried it around the pool all summer like a queen.

"I'm winning that trophy this year," Priya announced now, stretching against the chain-link fence. "My grandma's coming. She thinks I'm bad at sports." Priya's want was so loud Beatrice could practically see it in the air, glittering.

"Beatrice, you can't sprint the whole thing," her friend Milo called from the lifeguard chair, where he was selling juice boxes to spectators. "It's two laps, not one."

"I know that," Beatrice said. She did know it. The problem was that knowing and doing were two different animals. Then the wind gusted across the lot, rippling the pool beyond the fence, and Beatrice noticed something: the flags snapped hard on the back straight, right where the course curved past the deep end. Wind. That was a thing you had to fight. Fighting took energy. Energy was exactly what she'd been spending too early, like a kid who eats all the pizza before the guests arrive.

The starter raised a whistle. "Runners, two laps, first lap pacing!"

They took off, and Beatrice made herself hold back even though everything in her screamed to fly. On the back straight the wind hit her like an open oven door, molten air pushing against her chest. Priya was three steps ahead, arms pumping, cutting through it. So Beatrice slid in directly behind her, tucked close, and suddenly the push was gone, like walking behind a big kid in a hallway crowd.

"Quit following me!" Priya shouted over her shoulder.

"It's not personal!" Beatrice shouted back. "It's just easier back here!"

They came around into lap two, and Beatrice still had legs under her. Real legs, springy ones. She swung out on the final bend, the wind behind her now, and poured everything she had left into the straight. Priya's grandmother stood on a lawn chair screaming in two languages. Milo spilled a juice box. Beatrice hit the cone line half a step ahead and collapsed onto the hot asphalt, laughing.

Priya flopped down beside her, gasping. "Okay, teach me the following thing."

"Tomorrow," Beatrice said, staring up at the birdbath trophy gleaming on the picnic table. "Tomorrow I'm going to hold it over my head in the shallow end."

activity: to describe their family and pets in a new language using full sentences
story:
Rosalie sat near the window in Spanish class, tracing the edge of her notebook while Señora Vega wrote family words on the board. Outside, someone was pushing a mop across the courtyard, and the smell of floor cleaner drifted in through the cracked window. Today's assignment was to describe your family and pets in full sentences, out loud, in front of everybody. Rosalie had a dog named Baxter and no siblings, which made her sentences short and, she thought, a little boring.

Marisol went first. She stood up, folded her hands, and said, "Tengo dos hermanos y un gato."

"Two brothers and a cat," said Theo, translating for himself under his breath. "Lucky. I only have one hermana."

Marisol shook her head. "No, no. One brother, one sister."

Theo frowned at her. "But you said hermanos. Hermanos means brothers. So that's two brothers." He turned to Rosalie as if she were the judge of the class, which she found funny, since she had gotten a C minus on the last quiz.

Rosalie thought about it. She remembered the vocab list, and how "hermanas" had meant sisters, and "hermanos" had just been labeled brothers in her messy handwriting. But Marisol was from a family that spoke Spanish at home, and she didn't seem embarrassed or corrected, only impatient, like Theo was the one missing something obvious.

"Wait," Rosalie said slowly. She flipped back a page in her notebook. "Is it like, the plural hermanos can be brothers, or brothers and sisters together? So Tengo dos hermanos might be one brother and one sister?"

"Exactly," Marisol said, sounding relieved. "Two hermanos can be two boys, or a boy and a girl."

Theo sat back, still skeptical. "That seems confusing. How do you know which one somebody means?"

"You ask," Mariola said with a shrug, and the girl next to her laughed.

When it was Rosalie's turn, she stood and gave her sentences one by one. "Tengo un perro. Se llama Baxter." Then, feeling bold, she added, "No tengo hermanos," and she liked how it sounded, like a small complete picture of her life. After class, Theo cornered her at the door with a question about how the plural worked, and instead of explaining, Rosalie pulled out her notebook. "Say your sentence," she told him. "I want to hear if it sounds plausible."

"Um. Tengo dos hermanos," Theo said.

Rosalie grinned and raised one eyebrow, exactly the way Marisol had. "Interesting. Which kind?"

story:
Wyatt had been beating the same six guys all summer, but every single time trial ended the same way: first place for four hundred metres, then legs like wet noodles, then guys streaming past him on the final curve. Today, at the cracked courts behind Riverside Park, he meant to fix that. His friend Marcus had marked a rough four-hundred-metre loop with chalk arrows on the pavement, starting at the fence by the basketball court and winding around the tennis courts and back, and the two of them had agreed to run it twice without stopping.

"Warm-up lap, then we go," Marcus said, bouncing a basketball against the asphalt while Wyatt jogged in place. "My brother's timing us. He's got his phone out."

Wyatt's whole chest felt tight with wanting. The county meet was in three weeks, and the coach had told him plainly that raw speed wasn't his problem. The problem was invisible, hiding somewhere in that second lap, and nobody had been able to point at it.

They took off, sneakers slapping the chalky concrete, sun heating the back of Wyatt's neck. He felt fantastic, arms pumping, the wind pushing past his ears, and he flew around the far turn past the chained-up tennis gate. As he came through the loop's first marker, Marcus's brother cupped his hands and shouted, "Fifty-eight seconds!"

Wyatt grinned and surged harder. Marcus was already three steps behind, breathing hard. But somewhere on the second lap, Wyatt's legs went strange, heavy and slow, like running through deep sand at the lake. Marcus, who had started slower, came past him with a hundred metres left and beat him by four seconds.

They collapsed onto the hot court, and Wyatt stared at the peeling green backboard while his lungs burned. "Fifty-eight," he said. "That's what he yelled at the halfway mark. What is that number, exactly?"

"That's your split," Marcus said, still gasping. "The time for one section of the race. Halfway in an eight hundred is four hundred, so fifty-eight is your four-hundred split."

Wyatt sat up so fast his head spun. That was it. The number had been sitting there all along, waving at him. "I run my four hundred in fifty-eight when I time-trial a four hundred alone," he said. "So today my first lap was as fast as a flat-out race. That's why the second lap fell apart. It shows right away whether the first lap was faster or slower than planned, and mine was way too fast."

They ran it again before the sun got any higher. This time Wyatt kept his face neutral and his legs steady, refusing to let the easy spring in his knees propel him out front. The shout came at the halfway mark: "Sixty-eight!" Wyatt almost laughed out loud, because sixty-eight felt almost lazy, and he still had two guys in front of him. Then, at the final curve, he found energy he had never once had there before, passed Marcus with fifty metres to go, and crossed the chalk line with his fists in the air.

"Marcus!" he yelled, spinning around. "Tell your brother to call out my split again tomorrow. Same time, same place."

activity: to compare the climate of a desert and a rainforest using rainfall and temperature graphs
story:
Kayla's boots crunched on the gravel trail as she waved two crumpled printouts in the air like victory flags. "Okay, Dad, this is the hike where I finally figure out my climate project. Desert versus rainforest. Prepare to be amazed."

"You've said that three times since the parking lot," Dad said, swatting at a fly. "Once while holding a granola bar in the exact same way."

"Because the graphs are confusing!" Kayla stopped at a flat rock beside the trail and spread her pages in the sun. One graph showed the desert: rainfall bars so tiny they looked like a row of stubby teeth, temperatures high all year. The other showed the rainforest: fat rainfall bars stacked tall every single month. "Look at this. Both places are hot. The desert gets some rain. Not zero. So why is one a desert and the other a jungle? That's the part I keep getting wrong."

Dad sat down on a log and pretended to fall asleep, then peeked with one eye. "Wake me when you clarify something."

"You're hilarious." But the word snagged in her mind. Clarify. She stared at the two graphs until they blurred, and then something else surfaced, a memory from her cousin's house in Arizona, the summer she was nine. She'd dumped a bucket of water on the back patio to make a puddle to splash in, and by the time she came back outside after lunch, the concrete was bone dry. Not damp. Dry, like the puddle had never existed. The sun and the hot, dry air had simply taken it.

Kayla sat up so fast she nearly slid off her rock. "Wait. The sun and dry air could evaporate way more water in a year than the rain that falls. Like, way, way more. That's what happened to my puddle!" She jabbed a finger at the desert graph. "It doesn't matter that some rain falls, because the air takes back more than the sky gives. The ground stays dry. The rainforest graph is the opposite. The air can't take it as fast as it falls." She flipped between the pages so fast one nearly flew off the rock. "That's the whole answer. I was only counting what fell, not what vanished."

"That's quite a stanza of triumph," Dad said, nodding at her notebook, where she'd scribbled her idea in giant letters.

"That's not a stanza, that's a paragraph. Stanzas are poems."

"Then write it as a poem. 'Ode to a Vanished Puddle.'"

Kayla laughed so hard a jay scolded them from a manzanita bush. She grabbed her pencil, wrote "The Puddle Experiment" at the top of a fresh page, and underlined it twice. "I'm going to draw the bucket, the patio, and the dry concrete, right next to the rainfall bars. My teacher always says don't just be conventional with the visuals." She packed the graphs into her backpack with the ceremony of someone storing treasure, slung it over her shoulders, and pointed up the trail. "Race you to the switchback. Loser carries the water, which, for the record, I promise not to evaporate."

activity: to draw a street using one-point perspective with lines meeting at a vanishing point
story:
Lea sat on the floor of Grandpa's attic with a pencil, a ruler, and a photograph of her own street, because he had promised that if she learned to draw it "properly," he would let her paint the attic window frames however she wanted. That was mandatory, as far as she was concerned. No slanted lines, no crooked doors, no houses leaning like drunks. Grandpa had a whole shelf of art books up here, and he said the secret was something called perspective.

"Pick a spot," he said, shuffling past her with a box of old postcards. "One spot where every line runs to."

Lea stared at her blank page. One spot. She pressed the pencil tip down in the middle of the paper and made a small dark dot, then drew the street's edges slanting toward it, top lines down, bottom lines up. She added doorways and windows and let every edge lean inward like the whole street was being pulled by a magnet. "It's like everything's falling toward the dot," she said.

"Leonardo did that," Grandpa said from behind the postcards. He didn't turn around. "In the Last Supper. Every line in the whole painting runs to one single point, and that point sits right at Christ's head."

Lea frowned. "In the actual painting? How do you even know where that is after five hundred years?" She imagined the famous wall, the long table, all those lines of ceiling and tapestry invisible to anyone just looking.

Grandpa finally turned. "Because they found a nail hole there. Leonardo hammered in a nail and stretched strings from it to guide his lines, and the hole is still visible, right at Christ's head."

"A nail hole survived?" Lea said. She felt like she'd been handed testimony from a witness at the scene. A tiny hole, a mark you could stand in front of today. She looked down at her own dark dot and had an idea she could actually test. She found a pushpin in Grandpa's desk drawer and pressed it exactly into her dot, then tied a loop of thread around it.

"Now watch," she said, and pulled the thread taut along each line of her street, snapping a bit of graphite onto the string and flicking it so it left a straight gray ghost of a line. Lines she'd drawn crooked showed themselves instantly, bowing away from the pulled thread like liars. She erased and re-drew them, checking each one against the string, until every edge obeyed. The street on her page straightened itself into a real place, deep and solid, with her own front porch halfway down it.

Grandpa leaned over her shoulder and whistled. Lea pulled the pushpin out and held it up to the light, a tiny silver nail with a thread still looped around it. "I'm keeping this," she said. "It's going in the middle of the painting I do someday."

activity: to draw a street using one-point perspective with lines meeting at a vanishing point
story:
The art studio smelled like pencil shavings and old coffee, and Livia loved it anyway. She had claimed the stool by the window because the light there made her paper glow, almost transparent, so she could see the faint lines she'd already erased. Today Ms. Okafor had pinned a photograph of a narrow city street to the corkboard and told everyone, "Draw your orthogonals first."

Livia stared at her blank page. Orthogonals. The word sat in her head like a locked box. Ms. Okafor had already moved on to help Mateo, who was shading a bicycle, so Livia couldn't ask without losing her window seat. She squinted at the photograph instead. Somewhere on that street, the road edges angled toward each other. The curbs did too. She traced the two curb lines with her finger in the air, and they met somewhere far back, near the corner of the photo where the buildings got small. The rooflines, she noticed, tilted the same way, sliding down toward that same invisible meeting point.

"So the orthogonals are the lines that run back toward it," she whispered. "Road edges. Curbs. Rooflines." She wasn't sure, but it was a testable idea. She drew a small dot near the middle of her page, then let her ruler fan four lines out from it like ribs. Around those ribs she built the street: a curb here, a curb there, a slanted rooftop, a shop awning that conveniently leaned the way her lines went.

The drawing looked almost like a street. Almost. The awning on the left side stuck out wrong, floating like it didn't belong to any building. Livia frowned at it, then at her orthogonals, then at the awning again. She had ignored the line from the dot through the awning's corner. She erased it, laid the ruler from the vanishing point out through that corner, and rebuilt the awning along the ruler's edge. This time it sat on the building like it had grown there.

Behind her, a smaller kid named Priya was quietly crumpling her paper. "Mine looks like it's falling over," Priya said.

"Mine did too, until I started with the lines that go back to the dot," Livia said. She slid her pencil across the table so it rolled to a stop beside Priya's hand. "Try the curbs first. And the rooflines. They all point the same way."

Priya flattened her paper and made a dot of her own.

Ms. Okafor passed behind them and paused. "Careful," she said, tapping the corner of Livia's page, where too much erasing had started to erode the paper into a soft gray hole. "Even a good drawing can only survive so much fixing."

"That's a metaphor for something," Livia said, grinning.

"It's a warning about your paper," said Ms. Okafor, but she was smiling too. She picked up Livia's drawing and held it at arm's length, and Livia watched her eyes travel down the street, along the curbs, over the rooftops, all the way back to the dot. "Hang this one on the wall."

Livia wrote her name in the corner and carried it to the empty spot beside the window.

activity: to look at onion skin cells under a microscope and label the cell wall, membrane and nucleus
story:
Chloe had one weekend to finish her science project, and the only microscope on the farm belonged to her uncle's old science kit, kept in a box marked "Randy, 1987." Her plan was simple: cut a piece of onion, put it under the lens, and draw the cell wall, the cell membrane, and the nucleus for her labeled diagram. She sliced a thick wedge from the onion in the kitchen, carried it out to the porch on a saucer, and laid it on the glass slide. Through the eyepiece she saw nothing but gray darkness, like a window painted shut.

"You're doing it wrong," said her cousin Dana from the porch steps, where she was supposed to be shelling peas and mostly wasn't. "That thing's a piece of junk. Randy's microscope is older than my mom."

"It's not junk," Chloe said. "It's legitimate lab equipment. It has three magnification settings." But she frowned at the dark circle anyway. She flipped to the lowest setting. Still dark. The highest. Still dark. The onion was the problem, and she was starting to think so too, which was exactly what Dana wanted to hear.

That night Chloe wrote an email to her science teacher, because emailing a teacher at nine on a Friday felt less scary than calling one. "Dear Ms. Okafor," she typed, "I can't see any cells in the onion. My slide is just black. Is my microscope broken, or am I? Sincerely, Chloe, who has until Monday." Then she sat looking at the onion wedge on the counter, its rings like a tree stump in cross section, and something snagged in her mind. A microscope needed light to pass through a thing to see it. A thick wedge would block light the way a wall blocks a flashlight beam. What she needed was a piece thin enough for light to go through. She peeled the onion apart, layer by layer, and inside, where the rings curved tight and pale, she found a skin as fine as tissue paper. She pulled it loose with tweezers, dropped it in a drop of water, and lowered the cover slip.

"There," Dana said the next morning, leaning over the microscope on the porch. "Told you. Nothing there." Then she stopped. The field of view was full of cells, row after row of neat rectangles, like bricks in a wall, each with a darker dot floating inside it. "Whoa," Dana said. "That was not what I expected to say."

"That's the nucleus," Chloe said, pointing at the dot. "And the outside edge, the stiff line, that's the cell wall. The membrane is just inside it, thin like a skin of the skin." She drew each cell in her notebook and labeled the parts, then set up her control the way Ms. Okafor had taught them: the thin skin on one slide, the thick wedge on another, light the one variable she changed. She took photographs to document both slides, dark and bright, side by side.

On Monday, Ms. Okafor wrote back at last. "Chloe, your email arrived during my commute, but it sounds like you solved it before I even opened it. The thin inner skin of an onion is only one cell thick, so light passes through it and single cells can be seen under a microscope. Nice work." Dana read the email over Chloe's shoulder on the bus and jabbed a finger at the screen. "See? One cell thick. I'm telling everyone I helped."

"You shelled zero peas," Chloe said, and handed her the notebook to hold.

activity: to stand up for a classmate being teased without making the situation worse
story:
The three o'clock bus smelled like rain and pencil shavings, and Brooklyn had her usual seat, third from the back on the left, where the afternoon sun came through the window in a molten stripe across the vinyl. She was flipping through her history notes when the sound started up ahead of her: Dara Voss laughing her bright, too-loud laugh, and then Marcus saying something Brooklyn couldn't quite hear, and then a smaller voice, Ned's, saying, "It wasn't like that."

By the time the bus lurched around the corner by the pharmacy, Brooklyn had worked out the shape of it. Marcus was doing voices from the science fair, and every time he did Ned's voice, the high squeaky one, he paused and glanced back at the row where Dara and her friends sat. They laughed every single time. Ned laughed too, quick and thin, like he was paying a toll.

Brooklyn watched the pattern through two more stops. Marcus made the joke, Marcus looked at Dara's row, Dara's row delivered the laugh, and Marcus came back stronger, louder, the squeaky voice climbing higher. Ned's own laughter got smaller each round. It reminded her of the opposite of grade inflation, the way his pretending-to-enjoy-it was shrinking in value while the teasing ballooned.

She tried an experiment on herself first. When Marcus did the voice again, she caught her own face starting to smile, that reflex smile people wear just to fit in, and she smoothed it flat. Nothing happened. Nothing was supposed to. The laughers were the engine, and she was only ever a passenger in that part of the bus.

Then she did the harder version. On the next joke, when Marcus glanced back at Dara's row, Brooklyn leaned forward across the aisle and spoke to Dara, not to Marcus. "Hey, Dara, didn't you say you had extra cookies from the bake sale?" Dara blinked, then dug into her backpack, and the whole row got busy passing a napkin back and forth, and the laugh that Marcus was waiting for never arrived.

He did the voice once more, quieter, and looked back again, and got nothing but the back of Brooklyn's head. Then he tried a different topic, something about the gym teacher, and nobody fed that either. Brooklyn watched his shoulders drop about an inch. She kept her eyes on Dara's napkin, because looking at him would be a prize too.

At the last stop before hers, Ned slid into the empty seat beside her. He still had his poster tube from the science fair, bent at one corner. "Thanks," he said. "That was fast thinking."

"Sometimes it just needs the audience to stop clapping," Brooklyn said, and held the tube steady while he gathered his backpack, preserving the last unbent inch of it from the crushing crowd in the aisle.

"Tomorrow he'll probably just find something else," Ned said.

"Probably," Brooklyn said. "But I'll be riding this bus."

activity: to measure the speed of a rolling ball from distance and time and draw a distance-time graph
story:
Jayden had one goal at the science museum: beat the Rolling Racers exhibit. The rules said roll a ball down the ramp, and the screen drew a graph of your run. His best friend Priya had scored a straighter line than him twice already, and she would not stop mentioning it.

"Round three," Priya said, holding the red ball like a trophy she already owned.

Jayden set the ball at the top of the ramp, and his run looked the same as before: a line that started out nearly flat and then swept upward, curling steeper and steeper toward the corner of the screen. Priya's line did the same thing, just less. He'd been naive, he realized, thinking that letting go gently at the top would keep the line calm. The ball didn't care how gently he let go.

He grabbed the stopwatch and the tape measure the exhibit lent out, because the sign said you could measure the run yourself. Every half second, he marked where the ball was. One mark. Then another, farther. Then farther still, way farther. The gaps between his marks grew like the gaps between rungs on a crooked ladder. He plotted the marks on graph paper, one axis for time, one for distance, and the dots climbed into a curve that bent upward, steeper at the end than at the start. He stared at it. "The line isn't wrong," he said slowly. "The ball's actually going faster at the bottom. It's not messing up my graph. It's telling me something."

"So your line curves because your ball speeds up?" Priya leaned over his paper. "Then mine curves less because mine speeds up less?"

"Exactly. A line that curves upward and gets steeper means it's speeding up." He pointed at the screen. "So I've been trying to draw a straight line with a rolling ball. That's like trying to draw a circle with a ruler."

Priya laughed so hard a toddler at the next exhibit turned to stare. "Okay, curve master. I resign my title. But I get to hold the stopwatch for your next run."

Jayden rolled again, and this time he didn't fight the curve. He just watched it sweep up the screen, steep and proud, while Priya called out the times and the ball rolled on down the ramp.

activity: to compare simple and compound interest on a savings account over five years
story:
Blake wanted a mountain bike that cost two hundred eighty dollars, and his savings account held one hundred forty. He figured if he saved nothing more, the interest would grow his money until it covered the bike. At the kitchen table he spread out the bank statement, a pencil, and a bag of pretzels, and started working.

First he tried simple interest. Six percent of one hundred forty dollars was eight dollars and forty cents a year, so after five years he would have earned forty-two dollars. He wrote the total, one hundred eighty-two, and stared at it. That was not a bike. His little sister Nadia wandered in, snatched a pretzel, and leaned over his paper. "Why does your face look like that?" she asked.

He had to confess that his plan had a hole in it. "I thought the money would double," he said. "It won't. Not even close." Then he remembered something his grandfather had said at Thanksgiving while carving the turkey: "The rule of 72 tells you how long money takes to double with compound interest. Divide 72 by the yearly percentage rate." Blake had barely listened at the time, mostly because he wanted the dark meat. Now he grabbed the pencil again. At 6 percent, 72 divided by 6 was 12. Twelve years. He would be twenty-five, with a driver's license and probably no interest in a mountain bike at all.

"But compound interest is different from simple," Nadia said, chewing. She had clearly been eavesdropping on his muttering. "With compound, the interest earns interest too, right? The bank statement should say which one you have." Blake flipped the paper over and searched the fine print, which was so small he had to hold it under the lamp, where the bulb was warm and the light smelled faintly of dust. The word compound appeared in a paragraph about interest capitalization. His account was compound after all, and at 6 percent his one hundred forty would double in about twelve years, which still meant no bike by summer.

He slumped, and Nadia patted his shoulder with greasy sympathy. "I have empathy for you," she said solemnly, "because I once saved for a hamster and the store only had fish." Blake laughed so hard he knocked over the pretzels. Then he picked up his pencil and made a new plan, explicit and exact at the top of a fresh page: eight dollars a month from mowing lawns, plus the interest, bike money in one year, not twelve. He circled the number, folded the paper, and put it in his back pocket. Then he went outside to ask Mr. Delgado about his grass.

activity: to build a debate case with a claim, evidence and a warrant for each point
story:
Kaitlyn spread her debate notes across the front row of the auditorium, and her partner Marcus dropped into the seat beside her with a grin. Their first tournament was in four days, and their case about school start times was still a mess.

"I'm telling you, later start times help kids," Marcus said, tapping the page. "It's obvious."

"It's not obvious to a judge," Kaitlyn said. "Mrs. Reyes kept writing 'why?' next to every single thing you said yesterday." She flipped to the back of her notebook, where she'd copied something off the whiteboard after practice. "Okay, so there's this model. She wrote that the claim is the point being argued, and the grounds or data are the evidence given to support it."

"So I need grounds."

"We both do. Right now we have, like, six claims and zero grounds."

They tried it out loud. Marcus made his point about sleep, and Kaitlyn played the judge. "What's your evidence?" she asked, and Marcus froze. "You presume I'll just believe you," she added, "but a judge won't presume anything."

They dug through the crate of articles Mrs. Reyes kept in the auditorium's storage room. Marcus found a study about grades improving with later starts; Kaitlyn found attendance numbers from a district that had changed its schedule. Then she noticed something. Even with evidence in hand, Marcus's points still felt shaky, like a bridge missing its middle section.

"Watch," she said. She stood up on the stage to test it. "Claim: our school should start at eight-thirty. Grounds: in the district that shifted its start time, tardies dropped and grades went up." She paused. "But why does that evidence prove my point? Because when kids aren't half asleep, they show up and learn better. That connects them."

"That's the missing piece," Marcus said. "The warrant."

"Mrs. Reyes called it that. Claim, grounds, warrant. Every point needs all three or it falls apart."

They rebuilt the whole case, point by point, standing on the stage under the work lights. Marcus argued, Kaitlyn challenged, and when he nailed a tricky one, she said, "The judge would buy that," which made him punch the air. Halfway through, Mrs. Reyes came in to lock up, listened for a minute from the back, and didn't say a word, just gave them a thumbs-up and held the door.

At the tournament on Saturday, Marcus leaned over during the opponent's speech and whispered, "They're doing what we used to do. All claims, no grounds."

Kaitlyn uncapped her pen. "Then let's show them how it's done."

activity: to read the periodic table and find the number of protons in an element from its atomic number
story:
Rosalie stared at the giant periodic table taped above the science room window and felt like it was staring back. Mr. Patel had promised a quiz at the end of the period, and the class had exactly twenty minutes to figure out one thing: how to find the number of protons in any element. Nobody was allowed to ask him. "You have the whole table," he'd said, grinning. "It's all right there."

She narrowed her eyes at the boxes. Some had tiny numbers in the corners. Carbon had a 6 in one corner, and a 12 somewhere else, which felt like the table was trying to hinder her with extra numbers. Why would one box need two?

Her friend Dex leaned over, holding his pencil up like evidence. "This says graphite. That's what's inside the pencil. I looked it up, and graphite is carbon." He jabbed his finger at the carbon box. "So what's the little 6 mean? Six of what?"

Rosalie ran her finger along the row. Hydrogen had a 1. Helium had a 2. Lithium, 3. The numbers went up in order, one by one, all the way across the whole chart, like seats in a theater. "It's not random," she said slowly. "It's numbered. Like a list." She tapped the helium box. "And Mr. Patel called it the atomic number. He said it once, fast, when he taped this up Monday." Dex squinted at her, so she said it again, plain: "Atomic number. That's what the little number is called."

They tested it on paper. Rosalie wrote hydrogen, then a 1, then one proton. Helium, 2, two protons. If the pattern held for every box, then carbon, with its 6, had to have six protons in its nucleus, and every single carbon atom anywhere, in Dex's pencil, in diamonds, in her own bones, would have that same six. She looked up at the ceiling and wondered whether the graphite in Dex's pencil and the diamond in somebody's ring were, proton-wise, exactly the same. "Six protons in your pencil," she told him, and he held it out like it had suddenly become more interesting.

She copied her rule onto a notecard, then flipped it over and checked the oxygen box. 8. Eight protons. Sodium, 11. Eleven. It was like a principle hiding in plain sight, a rule the whole chart obeyed.

The timer buzzed. Mr. Patel walked the rows dropping quizzes face down, and when he reached Rosalie he set hers down and paused. "Question one," he read off his own sheet, half smiling. "A meteorite lands containing an element with atomic number 6. How many protons does each atom have?" Rosalie grinned at Dex. Carbon. Six protons. All that panic, and the first answer was sitting right there in his hand. She picked up her pencil and wrote the number 6.

activity: to change a flat bicycle tyre using tyre levers and a pump
story:
Hudson wheeled his bike through the door of the Suds and Spin, past the folding tables and a row of humming dryers, because the parking lot outside was the only flat stretch of pavement nearby and he had a flat tyre to prove it. His friend Marisol was already there, waiting on her aunt's laundry with a paperback and a bag of pretzels. "Snakebite puncture," she said, looking at the two small holes near the valve. "You hit the curb by the bus stop, didn't you."

"Maybe," Hudson admitted. He laid the bike on the tile floor, flipped it over, and crouched beside it. He had never changed a tyre before. His dad had said he could learn it himself, and had handed him tyre levers, a spare tube, and a pump that lived at the bottom of his backpack like a metal snake. The levers were flat plastic scoops, and it took him three tries to figure out that they slid between the tyre and the rim, then hooked onto spokes to hold the bead wide. "You look like you're performing surgery," Marisol said, and he laughed so hard one lever popped loose.

He found the holes in the old tube by holding it near his wet forearm and feeling for the cool breath of escaping air, a trick he had overheard at the bike shop and never believed until now. The new tube went in soft and floppy, and he tucked the tyre back into the rim with his thumbs, which took longer than it should have and made his hands ache in a satisfying way. Then came the pump. He worked the handle, watching the tyre fatten a little with each stroke, and stopped when it looked done. "Fifty pounds," he announced, feeling the sidewall with his palm. "That sounds about right."

Marisol pressed the tyre with one finger and it dimpled like a loaf of bread. "Fifty what? It feels soft." Hudson frowned. He had made the number up, and now the tyre itself was quietly disagreeing with him. He spun the wheel slowly, checking for anything he might have missed, and on the black rubber of the sidewall, in small raised letters, he found grey words half worn away. He tilted the wheel toward the window light. "Inflate to 65 psi," he read out loud. "Psi. It's printed right on the tyre." The number was there all along, waiting where nobody looks, like the answer printed upside down at the bottom of a puzzle page.

He went back to pumping, counting strokes out loud, checking with his palm every so often until the tyre felt firm as a drum. Marisol tried pressing it and raised her eyebrows. "Okay, that's different." Hudson flipped the bike upright and rolled it a few feet, listening to the tyre tick over the tile. A woman at the change machine watched them with a small smile, and the folding tables smelled faintly of detergent. "All this free learning," Marisol said, "in a place built for commerce." Hudson clipped the pump shut and slung his backpack over one shoulder. "Same time next puncture," he said, and wheeled the bike out into the sun.

activity: to read the rights listed in their country's constitution or charter and explain one in their own words
story:
Clara had come to her grandmother's house planning to finish her social studies assignment, but her cousin Dex had other ideas. He stood in the kitchen holding a marker he'd found in the junk drawer, grinning at the paper tablecloth Grandma kept for Sunday dinners.

"Freedom of expression," Dex announced, uncapping the marker. "It's in the Charter. Means anyone can say anything, draw anything, anywhere. I could write on this tablecloth and the government can't stop me."

"That's not how it works," Clara said, though she wasn't sure how it did work. She was skeptical of anything Dex declared so loudly, because last summer he'd sworn that the water tower was full of money and half the neighborhood kids had climbed the fence before Mr. Petrelli chased them off. Still, her assignment was due Monday, and all she had so far was a blank page titled Rights and Freedoms.

Grandma's copy of the Charter lived on the shelf beside the TV guide, a thin paperback with a cracked spine. Clara pulled it down and flipped to the beginning, because if you were going to argue about rights, she figured you should start where the document started. Section 1 sat right there on the first page of rights. She read it twice, then a third time, moving her lips.

"Listen," she said. "Section 1 of the Canadian Charter says its rights are subject to reasonable limits that can be demonstrably justified in a free and democratic society."

Dex froze with the marker an inch above the tablecloth. "Subject to what?"

"Reasonable limits. Limits that can be demonstrably justified. It means the rights have a border around them, kind of." Clara tapped the page. "So 'freedom of expression' isn't a wall you can hide behind. It's more like a field with a fence."

Grandpa shuffled in from the porch, where he'd been listening, Clara realized, the whole time. He was a veteran who kept his old army photographs in a shoebox and never made speeches about any of it. He picked up the paperback and looked at Section 1, and Clara remembered the day two winters ago when he'd stood at the window watching the neighbors' protest march go by with signs and drums. She'd asked him then if all that noise was allowed, and he'd only said, "It's allowed because it's peaceful. That's the fence." She hadn't understood him then. She understood him now.

"You were going to obstruct Grandma's dinner," Grandpa said mildly, nodding at the marker. He didn't say anything else. He set the book back on the shelf and went to pour his coffee.

Dex looked at the tablecloth, at the marker, at the shelf. He capped the marker and put it back in the drawer, then pulled out a chair for Clara and slid the empty butter dish aside to make room for her notebook.

"So," he said, sitting down across from her. "What's this assignment? Explain a right in your own words?"

"Freedom of expression," Clara said, and opened to a clean page. "I think I finally have something to write."

"Write fast," Dex said, jerking his thumb toward the window. "Grandma's car is pulling in."

activity: to draw a street using one-point perspective with lines meeting at a vanishing point
story:
Zack taped his sketch to the kitchen table so it wouldn't slide, then leaned over it with his pencil hovering. The drawing showed the main road from summer camp, the one that ran straight past the mess hall toward the lake. His road looked wrong, though. Both edges slanted inward like they might crash into each other, and the sidewalk lines wandered off in their own directions, headed for three different spots on the paper.

He remembered the last afternoon of camp, standing on that road with the hot asphalt smell rising around his sneakers and the sun baking the back of his neck. His cabin mate Dylan had sketched the same road in ten minutes flat, and it had looked so real you could almost hear the gravel crunch. Zack had stuffed his own crooked attempt into his duffel bag before anyone could see it. Now, three weeks later, he wanted to get it right before Dylan visited on Saturday. He had one shot, and he intended to win it, because Dylan had a total monopoly on being the artist in their cabin and Zack was done with that.

He grabbed a fresh sheet and tried again from memory. He could hear the cicadas from that afternoon, feel the way the heat shimmered over the far end of the road. He drew the road, then two rows of buildings, then the sidewalk lines. Still crooked. Still three separate spots where things seemed to aim.

Zack flattened Dylan's camp sketch on the table beside his own and grabbed a ruler. He lined the ruler up with one edge of Dylan's road and drew the line longer with a light pencil stroke. He did the same with the other edge. Then the sidewalk lines, one after another. His heart started thumping, because every single line ran to the same exact point. He checked the other side of the street next, the rooflines, the shop windows. All of them, all of it, straight to that one dot.

"It's one point," he said out loud to the empty kitchen. "Every line going back meets at one point." He noticed the dot sat exactly on the line where Dylan had drawn the distant horizon, and he held the sketch up to his own eye level, squinting. It was even with his eyes when he stood. "A vanishing point," he said, trying the words out. "On the horizon line. At eye level."

He started a new drawing, and this time he placed the dot first, then the horizon, then let every line obey. The road opened up in front of him, wide at the bottom and narrowing toward that single faraway point, and the street looked like you could walk right into it. He added an intricate shopfront with carved trim and a striped awning, keeping every edge aimed home. When he finished, he held the paper at arm's length and grinned. The details implied a whole town beyond the last building, a street that kept going somewhere he couldn't see.

The doorbell rang Saturday morning before Zack even heard a car pull in. He ran to answer it with the sketch still in his hand, and Dylan stood on the porch, blinking at it.

"Whoa," Dylan said. "You drew that?"

Zack stepped back and held the paper up to his own eye level, right in front of Dylan's face. "Every line goes to one vanishing point. Want to see?"

Grandpa's bobber sat on the water like a small red apple, and Austin watched it while his dad, back at the cabin, banged a cabinet door shut for the third time that morning. Dad had quit chewing tobacco on Monday, and by Thursday nobody in the family wanted to be near him. Austin had come fishing mostly to escape.

"Your dad hollered at the coffee maker," Grandpa said, casting his line near the lily pads. "Didn't know a coffee maker could do anything wrong."

"He hollered at me for breathing loud," Austin said. "I wasn't even breathing loud." He turned his rod a little, watching the line sink and then submerge as the current took the bobber under for a second before it popped back up. He had started keeping a list in his notebook that week, because lists helped him think. Monday: Dad snapped about the thermostat. Tuesday: Dad couldn't finish a crossword and threw the pencil. Wednesday: Dad paced the porch and said he couldn't sit still, then snapped at Grandpa's old dog for existing.

"Been like that all week," Austin said. "Like he's a different person."

Grandpa reeled in, slow and patient. "My granddad, your great-great, he farmed tobacco for a stretch. Every descendant in the family has had some brush with the stuff, one way or another." He said it plainly, like he was talking about the weather, and cast again near the reeds.

Austin turned his notebook sideways and looked at his list. Snapping. Can't concentrate. Jumpy and anxious. And twice he'd caught Dad staring at the empty pocket where the tin used to be, jaw working, like he wanted it so bad his teeth ached. Those were cravings, strong ones. Austin had a hunch, and a hunch was like a fishing spot: you had to test it before you trusted it. So that afternoon he did a simple thing. He made a chart with columns for grumpy, anxious, can't-focus, and craving, and he marked what he saw, hour by hour, all four showing up again and again, day after day.

At dinner he slid the chart across the table to his mother. "I think it's withdrawal," Austin said. "When a person who's dependent stops nicotine, withdrawal can bring irritability, anxiety, trouble concentrating, and strong cravings. All four. Every day this week."

Dad set his fork down. He looked at the chart for a long moment, at the columns of little tally marks lined up against his name. "So it's not just me being a jerk," he said.

"It's a thing," Austin said. "It has a name."

Dad pulled the rubber band off the morning newspaper and stretched it between his fingers, elastic and tight, then let it shrink back. "All four, huh. Every day." He wrapped the band around his wrist. "Then I can count the days, too. Starting with this one."

He picked his fork back up and asked Grandpa to pass the potatoes.

Dev turned the wheel with one finger, and the wedge with "animal" on it passed under his thumb and came around again. "Karma does. It's like a chain. Evelyn's science fair project was due on Friday, and on Wednesday it consisted of a battery, a coil of nichrome wire, a voltmeter, an ammeter, and a blank sheet of graph paper that seemed to be cherishing its blankness. Her best friend Ruby stood beside the lab table eating pretzels.

"So what's it supposed to prove?" Ruby asked.

"That I can measure something I can't see." Evelyn clipped the meters into place and wrote down her first reading: 0.4 volts, 0.2 amps. She adjusted the battery pack, took another. Then another, until five pairs of numbers sat in her notebook like five unrelated facts.

"Great," said Ruby. "Five facts."

"That's the problem." Evelyn tapped the notebook. "Every reading is slightly different. Which one is the resistance? I can't exactly look inside the wire."

Ruby offered her a pretzel, which she declined. Evelyn stared at the numbers instead. Each voltage divided by its current gave roughly two: 0.4 over 0.2, 1.0 over 0.5, 1.6 over 0.8. Roughly, but not exactly, because her meters wobbled and her hands weren't steady. She had five noisy answers where she wanted one clean one.

She grabbed the graph paper and plotted all five points, voltage up the side, current along the bottom. Then she leaned close. The points weren't scattered. They fell along a slanted line, and if she pushed that line far enough in her mind, it went through zero: no current, no voltage, sitting together at the corner like two shy kids at a dance.

"Oh," she said.

"Oh what?"

"Look." She laid her ruler along the points. "The line goes straight through zero. And the slope, how steep it is, that's the resistance." She measured it against her axes. Two ohms. Five wobbly readings had become one answer that none of them, alone, had actually given her.

On Friday the judge read her graph, looked at her table of data, and nodded twice. Evelyn decided this was testimony enough, though she would have accepted a ribbon too. Ruby, watching from the next aisle, was grinning with an enthusiasm that proved infectious; two sixth graders came over to ask what the ruler was for.

"Measuring the slope," Evelyn said, and slid the graph across the table.

"You're doing homework at a skate park," Marcus said, rolling to a stop beside her.

"It's not homework, it's an experiment." She clipped the meter's probes to each end of the wire and touched the battery leads on. "See, this wire has 6 volts across it. "So flip it," Marcus said.

"Divide instead." She swept the chalk through the 12 and worked it out. "6 divided by 2. That's 3 ohms." The number sat there on the concrete, small and tidy, and it made sense to her the way a landed trick made sense, everything fitting at once. "Three! That has to be it. It matches the wire. Twelve didn't."

Marcus planted his board upright in the dirt. "How do you know for sure?"

"Because the strange answer was the clue. When I multiplied, I got something weird, so the rule has to run the other way." She wanted to assess the idea properly, not just trust it, so she pulled a second piece of wire from the coil, a shorter one, and hooked it up the same way. New reading. She divided again, and again the answer came out reasonable, a small number for a small wire. "It works twice," she said, grinning so hard her cheeks hurt.

Up on the platform, two older skaters were watching, their synthetic deck tape glittering in the sun. One of them called down, "What are you two doing down there, math?"

"Kind of!" Gabriella held up her chalk, which was worn to a stub now. "This wire has 6 volts across it and 2 amps flowing through it, and I figured out its resistance is 6 divided by 2, which is 3 ohms!"

The skater pumped a fist in the air like she'd landed something. "All right," Marcus said, dragging her up by the elbow, "now drop in, genius. You've earned it."

The automatic doors of Ridgeline Pharmacy hissed shut behind Jeremy, sealing him into the smell of cough drops and floor polish. He was there for one reason: his grandfather's blood pressure pills, which meant he was there alone, because Gramps had been dizzy all morning and couldn't get off the couch. Jeremy had the prescription slip folded in his pocket like a secret.

The line at the counter was six people long. Behind him, an eccentric old woman in a purple raincoat, dry as a bone on this sunny day, hummed what sounded like a song from some ancient Chinese dynasty. Jeremy checked the slip again. Twelve minutes, the clock over the register said. His heart was hammering, fast and shallow, the way it did before a spelling bee.

He put two fingers on his wrist, the way Gramps had shown him, and counted. While he breathed in, the pulse ticked quick, quick, quick. While he let the air out, it dragged, slower, like it was wading through honey. He tried it again to be sure. In, faster. Out, slower. Every single time. So the heart speeds up a little on each breath in, he thought, and slows down a little on each breath out. Then a strange idea came to him: if he made the out-breath long, would the slow part last longer? Would his heart settle?

He breathed in for three counts and out for six. In, four. Out, eight, lips puckered like he was cooling soup. The purple raincoat woman stopped humming and watched him with interest. "You look like a bagpipe," she said. "My heart speeds up a little when I breathe in and slows down when I breathe out," Jeremy said, almost to himself. "So I'm making the out part long." He checked his wrist again. The hammering had softened into a steady, patient knock.

His phone buzzed. A text from Gramps: Jeremy. If the line is long, do not worry about me. I ate crackers and I am watching the game. The dizzy spell passed. Also there are cookies in the tin above the stove, and they signify that I am proud of you for going alone.

Jeremy read it twice. The dizzy spell had passed. He hadn't known that. All this time in line, he'd been imagining ambulances, and Gramps was watching the game and hiding cookies. His heart had been racing over a danger that was already gone.

"Next," the pharmacist called. Jeremy stepped up, slid the slip across the counter, and kept breathing out, slow and long, all the way to eight. The tin of cookies felt closer than it had all morning. "That'll be ten minutes," the pharmacist said, and Jeremy nodded, counting already, in through his nose, out through his pursed lips, the pulse in his wrist tapping along, calm as a metronome.

story:
Noah had a plan for summer at Grandpa's house: sleep until noon every single day, exactly like he did at home on Saturdays. But by the second week, something felt wrong. His head ached in the mornings, his stomach knotted up for no reason, and on the afternoon Grandpa asked him to help fix the fence, his hands shook so hard he dropped the hammer twice. "It's like my whole body is braced for something bad," Noah told Grandpa, "and I don't even know what." That night he found an old notebook and wrote down everything: when he woke, when his stomach hurt, when his hands shook. He wanted to isolate the problem, the way Grandpa isolated the bad spark plug in the truck by testing one wire at a time.

The notebook showed a pattern almost immediately. Bad mornings followed late nights. Great mornings followed nights when he'd gone to bed at ten and gotten up at eight, even once, on the day they went fishing. Noah stared at the page. It couldn't be that simple. Could going to bed at the same time really fix his shaky hands and twisted stomach? He decided to test it like a science experiment: same bedtime, ten o'clock, same wake-up, eight o'clock, every single day, weekends included. He wrote the rules in big letters and taped them above the guest bed, right next to a postcard from his friend Marcus.

Marcus's postcard had arrived that morning, and Noah read it again before bed. "Dear Noah," it said, "I got a concussion at baseball practice, so I have to sleep a LOT this month. The doctor says rest fixes brains. My rich uncle came to visit, he's super affluent, he bought me a new glove. Get this: I miss you, dude. Come home soon. P.S. my sister says snail mail is old. I say it's awesome." Noah smiled, folded the card into the notebook, and turned off the light at ten o'clock sharp, even though he wasn't tired.

Saturday was the real test. When eight o'clock came, Noah's body woke on its own, without an alarm, feeling like a door swinging open instead of a wall he had to push through. He made eggs for Grandpa, fixed two fence boards without dropping anything, and spent the afternoon building a birdhouse. Sunday, same thing. Monday, same thing. "Grandpa," he said, holding up the notebook at breakfast, "I think there's a clock inside me. When I keep my bedtime and wake-up the same every day, weekends too, everything runs smooth. When I don't, everything jams up."

Grandpa set down his coffee. "There is such a thing," he said. "It's called the circadian rhythm." Noah wrote the words in the notebook and underlined them twice, then flipped back through his pages of shaky-hand days and smooth days, tapping each one with his pencil. "Ten more days," he announced. "I'm running the experiment through the whole month, even when you want to watch the late movie with me." Grandpa laughed. "Then we'll record the movie," he said, "because I'm keeping that fence-repairing, egg-cooking Noah around." That night Noah set his homemade chart where he'd see it first thing: ten to eight, ten to eight, ten to eight.

Hazel stood on the back porch of Marisol's birthday party holding a paper plate with cake she hadn't touched, because the Robo-Rockets club was about to implode. Yesterday's meeting had been a disaster: forty minutes gone on arguing about snacks, and the bridge project never even came up. Then Priya had quit, loudly. Now half the club was here at the party, and if Hazel didn't fix it, the club was over by Monday.

"I say we just vote Priya back in and forget the whole thing," said Dexter, through a mouthful of frosting.

"Priya doesn't want to be voted back in," Hazel said. "She wants a turn to talk. So do the sixth graders. So does everybody, and nobody gets one, because we all just shout."

She had noticed a pattern across their last four meetings. Whoever talked loudest got the most time, and the quiet kids got nothing, which meant ideas were being lost before anyone even heard them. Something invisible was running the meetings, like a conductor nobody had hired. But if the problem was invisible, maybe the fix had to be written down where everyone could see it.

She set her plate on the railing. "New plan. Before Monday's meeting, I write a list of everything we need to discuss, in the order we'll discuss it. Bridge budget first, snack schedule dead last, so it can't eat the meeting again. Every topic gets a name next to it, and that person speaks first."

Dexter squinted. "What do we even call that? A list of rules?"

Hazel had looked it up that morning, expecting something boring, and found something better. "It's called an agenda," she said. "It's a Latin word. It means things to be done."

Dexter blinked. "Our meetings are being saved by ancient Romans?"

"Apparently." She pulled a folded paper from her back pocket, the draft she'd made during musical chairs. At the top she'd written AGENDA in letters so big they looked mildly deranged. "Look, if this is bizarre, tell me now, because I'm going to hand this out Monday."

Marisol leaned over her shoulder. "You put Priya down for the bridge update. First speaker."

"Because she'll actually say something worth hearing if we let her." Hazel chewed her pencil. "I might revise the order, though. Maybe snack schedule in the middle, as a reward."

Dexter looked at the paper for a long moment. "Okay," he said. "I take back the voting thing. Priya won't come back because we vote. She'll come back because there's a list with her name on it." He held out his hand for the pencil. "Let me write it. My handwriting is less bizarre than yours."

Hazel laughed and handed it over. Behind them, someone started the piñata, and the porch filled with the sound of a paper dragon getting what it deserved.

Zack slid three books off the shelf and dropped them onto the study table by the window. His essay was due Friday, and he already knew his argument: video games improve focus and reflexes, with three points to prove it. He wrote his thesis at the top of a fresh page, then started making an outline. Point one, faster reaction time. Point two, better attention. Point three, improved memory.

Across the table, his neighbor Priya looked up from her own notebook. She was at the library every Tuesday because she wanted to win the county history contest, and she needed the reference section all to herself. "You look like you're building a fort out of index cards," she said.

"Outlining," Zack said. "Thesis first, then three points, then draft. Mr. Okafor's whole system." Priya rolled her eyes, and for a second Zack worried she would ridicule his neat numbered list the way some kids at school did. Instead she leaned over.

"Interesting," she said. "Keep going."

The first book said gamers had quicker reactions. Good. The second book, though, said heavy gaming was linked to worse attention in classrooms, and that "perceived focus" often faded after long sessions. Zack flipped pages faster, hunting for anything that matched his third point, but the memory studies were frail, small samples, contradictory results. He sat back. Had he picked the wrong argument entirely?

His intuition said to keep the thesis and just skip the bad sources. But skipping sources felt like hiding them. He remembered a poster above Mr. Okafor's desk from last semester: a pencil with an eraser the size of the pencil itself. Underneath it said something about a working thesis. A first thesis was called a working thesis because it could change, Mr. Okafor had told the class, and if the evidence pointed somewhere else, a careful writer revised the thesis instead of ignoring the evidence. Zack had thought the poster was decorative back then. Now he wondered whether the evidence was telling him something his outline hadn't planned for.

He crossed out his old thesis. Then he wrote a new one: video games sharpen some skills but may harm classroom attention, and the effect depends on how they're used. His three points rearranged themselves almost instantly, like the argument had been waiting to face the other direction. Priya read it upside down from her side of the table and tapped the crossed-out line.

"See?" she said. "That's why I never write my title first."

Zack laughed and pulled the eraser off his pencil.
