He called the meeting to order. "Item one," he said. "The telescope fundraiser." Denny immediately stood up and started describing a car wash, then a bake sale, then a plan to sell glow-in-the-dark planets at lunch, and Bentley watched Priya's hand rise halfway and sink again. Marcus leaned back and checked the clock. Two kids were already whispering about something else. Bentley recognized the pattern from last week: the louder Denny got, the more the room drained, until nobody was listening to anybody.

He raised his hand. "Hold on. New rule for today. We go around the circle, and each person speaks once before anybody speaks twice." Denny frowned. "What's that called?" "A round-robin," Bentley said. "Each person speaks in turn around the circle. It gives the quieter members a guaranteed chance to share their ideas." He pointed to Priya, who sat at the far end. "You're first."

Priya looked at her sneakers. Then she said, "The planetarium downtown does free shows for school groups on Thursdays. If we volunteer as guides for their kids' night, they said we could use their telescope for our Mars observations." The room went quiet in a good way. Marcus sat up. "Wait, their eighteen-inch telescope? That's significant. That's way better than the bake sale money." Denny, to his credit, nodded slowly. "That's the best idea of the meeting," he admitted, and Bentley wrote it at the top of the agenda board.

They planned it out in ten minutes flat, going around the circle twice more. Priya volunteered to email the planetarium director, since she was the one who knew her. Marcus offered to drive a carpool, and Denny, given his one turn, suggested they study the recession of the Andromeda galaxy's light as a backup project, which even Priya agreed was a decent idea.

When everyone had gone, Bentley pulled out his phone and typed a reply to his cousin. "It worked. The quiet one had the best idea." He paused before sending it, thinking about last week, when Priya had walked out with her bag over her shoulder and he'd said nothing. He'd never know what she might have offered then. "Next time," he typed instead, "she goes first every week." Then he erased the agenda, packed the markers, and turned off the lights.

activity: to build a debate case with a claim, evidence and a warrant for each point
story:
Lincoln sat in the third row of the school auditorium, glaring at his notebook. On Saturday his debate team had lost to Ridgeview, and tomorrow they had to face them again. Coach Reyes had written one comment on his notes: "Where's your warrant?" Lincoln knew how to make a claim, and he knew how to find evidence, but the warrant, the part that showed why the evidence proved the claim, kept slipping away from him like water in his fist.

His teammate Priya plopped into the seat beside him and slid a tablet across the armrest. "Watch the video from Saturday," she said. "Something's off about their closing." Lincoln pressed play. The Ridgeview captain stood at the podium in her navy blazer and told the judges that Lincoln's team wanted shorter recesses, so obviously they believed kids should have no recess ever, just worksheets from eight to three. The audience had laughed, and the judges had nodded along.

"That's not what we said," Lincoln muttered. He rewound and watched again. Their actual case was that fifteen minutes of recess instead of twenty would leave more time for science labs. Ridgeview had replaced that with the silliest version they could build and then knocked it over. He paused the video on a frame of the captain's smug smile. "They didn't beat our argument. They beat some fake argument wearing our argument's clothes."

"So we call it out," Priya said.

"First I need to see if it's a pattern," Lincoln said. He found two more Ridgeview debates online, one about school uniforms and one about the cafeteria menu. In both, the captain took the other team's reasonable claim, stretched it into something absurd, and attacked that instead. In the cafeteria debate, the other team had suggested one meatless lunch per week, and Ridgeview demanded to know why they wanted to make every student an unwilling herbervore. "It's her herbivore speech," Lincoln said, almost laughing. "She does this every single time. I can infer her whole strategy from three videos."

He flipped to a fresh page and rebuilt his case the way Coach Reyes kept drawing on the whiteboard. Claim: shorter recess improves learning. Evidence: the district study showing better focus after a balanced schedule. Warrant: the study measured exactly the change they were proposing, so the results applied. One clean chain for each point. Then, at the bottom, he wrote a question he would save for the rebuttal.

The next afternoon, under the auditorium's hot stage lights, the Ridgeview captain did exactly what Lincoln predicted. She asked the judges why his team hated fun and wanted to chain kids to their desks forever. Lincoln stood, gripped the sides of the podium, and kept his voice level. "That's a straw man argument. It misstates our position as something sillier, then attacks that version instead of our real one." He held up his notes. "Our real position, with claim, evidence and warrant, is right here. Attack that."

The lead judge leaned forward and said, "Please continue, and take your time."

activity: to cook rice, a curry and flatbread so they are all ready at the same time
story:
Lillian stood at the stove with three pans waiting and no plan. Her grandmother had always made Sunday dinner look easy, but Grandma was visiting her sister this weekend, and Lillian had promised the family a real meal: rice, curry, and flatbread, all hot at the same time.

The first attempt fell apart fast. She put the onions in the pan, then went hunting through the cupboard for cumin while they sizzled. By the time she found the jar, the kitchen smelled like burnt sugar and the onions were black. The rice water was boiling over. The flatbread dough was still stuck to the bowl. Her little brother Dev wandered in and sniffed the air.

"That smells like campfire," he said. "Is dinner going to be a candidate for the trash can?"

"Go set the table," Lillian said, but he had a point. She scraped the onions into the compost and stood there, thinking. The problem wasn't the recipe. The problem was what she couldn't see until it failed: everything moved too fast once heat touched food. The onions burned while she searched. She needed a rule for that, something like the one Grandma muttered in the kitchen. She called Grandma, who answered on the second ring.

"Of course it burned, sweetheart," Grandma said. "Mise en place. It's a French cooking term meaning 'putting in place': you prepare and measure every ingredient before you start cooking."

Lillian hung up and got to work. She diced two onions into a bowl, measured the cumin, turmeric, and coriander into a small dish, opened the can of coconut milk, and set the salt on the counter with a spoon in it. She tested her idea by laying everything in a row next to the stove, close enough to grab without stepping away. If the hidden cause of the burnt onions was searching, then removing the searching should remove the burning. She would find out.

This time, when the onions hit the oil, the spices were already at her elbow. She stirred, dumped them in on time, and poured the coconut milk without ever leaving the pan. Then she had to prioritize: the rice needed twenty minutes, the curry needed fifteen, and the flatbread cooked in two minutes per side, so the rice went first, the curry second, and she would roll the flatbreads while the curry simmered. Dev kept drifting back to the stove, and she finally put him in charge of tearing cilantro, which he pretended was a chore and secretly took seriously. He wanted to be the one who picked the toppings, and he arranged torn cilantro, yogurt, and lime wedges on a plate like medals.

When Dad came in, the table held three dishes steaming at once, all of them ready together. Dev pointed at his topping plate. "I made that."

"You made that," Lillian agreed, and slid the last flatbread off the pan onto the bread basket. "Sit down before it gets cold."

activity: to write a short story with correctly punctuated dialogue and a clear climax
story:
Claire had written the same sentence six times, and it still looked wrong. Mrs. Okafor had said the stories were due at the end of the period, and every story needed dialogue, a climax, and correct punctuation. Claire's story was about a girl named Ruby whose brother Marco had seen something growing on the cafeteria bread. That part was fine. The problem was the line where Ruby told her friend, "Marco said, 'It's a fungus.'"

She stared at the marks. Did a quote inside a quote get double marks again, or something else? Across the room, Devon was already printing his story, smug as anything. Claire refused to ask him. Last week he had told her "who" was always the subject of a sentence, and she had believed him for two days.

She flipped through her reading folder. In the short story they'd studied, "The Long Walk Home," a character named Aunt Ro repeated what the bus driver had told her. Claire found the page and ran her finger along the line. Aunt Ro said, "The driver told me, 'No more stops after nine.'" The driver's words sat inside single quotation marks, tucked within the double ones. She checked another story. Same pattern. A quotation inside another quotation used single marks within the double ones.

"Ten minutes," Mrs. Okafor called.

Claire tried it. Ruby leaned close and whispered, "Marco said, 'It's a fungus.'" It looked strange on the page, like a door inside a door, but the pattern held in both published stories, and Claire trusted a systematic check over a feeling. She kept going, building toward her climax: Ruby had to decide whether to warn the whole lunch line or stay quiet, because Marco had begged her not to start trouble.

Then she paused. Maybe the story was better if Ruby told the principal, and the principal organized a boycott of the cafeteria until the kitchen was inspected. Claire had been planning a quieter ending, but now that she saw Ruby as a girl who acted, she changed her mind and crossed out her old last page.

"Time's up," Mrs. Okafor said, walking down the rows.

Devon leaned over. "You know your ending's never going to happen, right? Nobody boycotts anything over bread."

Claire slid her paper to the corner of her desk, printed side up, single marks and all. "Read page two," she said. "Then tell me you'd eat the lunch."

activity: to compare a stock and a bond and explain which is riskier and why
story:
Joshua had one goal for Saturday: earn forty dollars at the lemonade stand so he could buy the used walkie-talkies from the flea market. He set up his table under the oak tree, squeezed the lemons until his hands smelled sour, and taped a sign that said COLD LEMONADE, ONE DOLLAR to the front. His little fan, which he used to regulate the temperature of the ice cooler, hummed beside the pitcher.

His friend Marcus pedaled up the street on his bike, but he didn't stop for lemonade. He stopped to talk, and his voice was flat in a way Joshua had never heard before. "You know that game company everybody was hyped up about? I put all my birthday money in the stock. Sixty dollars." He kicked at the curb. "The company failed. Completely. The stock went to zero." Joshua waited, because it sounded like there was more. "Zero means I lost every dollar, Josh. All sixty."

Joshua poured him a cup without asking for the dollar, because that seemed like the right thing to do. While Marcus drank, Joshua got out his notebook and drew two boxes. "Okay, so a stock is when you own a tiny piece of the company. If the whole company goes under, your piece isn't worth anything. It can just go to zero." Marcus nodded glumly. "But my sister's been telling me about bonds," Joshua went on. "A bond is more like you loaned the company money, and they owe you back."

"So if it fails, you still get paid?" Marcus asked.

Joshua chewed on that. "I think the stock is the riskier one. If the company dies all the way, the stockholder can lose every single dollar he put in. That's what just happened to you, so it's not just a theory." He tapped the second box. "The bond is a promise to repay, so it doesn't drop to nothing the same way."

Marcus sat up a little straighter. "Then I'm buying a bond with my allowance. And I'm not putting everything in one company ever again. Deal?"

"Deal." Joshua wrote it in the notebook and made them both sign it, like a contract. Then Mrs. Alvarez came by with her whole dog-walking network, six leashes and six thirsty owners, and the line for lemonade stretched past the mailbox. Joshua pumped the cooler fan to full speed, handed out cups, and watched his dollar total climb toward forty while Marcus, at the end of the table, made change and grinned at every customer who walked up.

activity: to solve linear equations with one variable by doing the same operation to both sides
story:
The crumpled receipt had been sitting in Noemie's pocket all morning, ever since her grandmother had thrust it at her at breakfast with an abrupt "Something is wrong with this, I know it." The taxi company had charged fifteen dollars for their ride to the library on Saturday, and Grandma insisted the meter was rigged. Noemie had watched the numbers flick past the whole way, but she could not remember how far they had actually gone.

In math class, Mr. Okafor had them balancing equations on the board, the same operation on both sides, an equals sign like a scale that must stay level. Noemie copied the method into her notebook and then sat tapping her pencil. Could the receipt be turned into an equation too? The taxi charged three dollars just to start, she remembered, plus two dollars for every kilometre. She wrote 3 + 2k = 15 and underlined the k. That little letter was supposed to symbolize the thing she wanted and did not know yet: the distance. Somewhere inside the equation, the answer was hiding like a coin under a cup.

Beside her, Marcus was chewing his pen and frowning at his own paper. He wanted the class contest prize, a compass for geometry, and he was two problems behind. "You get it, don't you," he muttered, not really a question. Noemie had compassion for his scrunched-up frustration, because last week she had been the one hiding her paper. She tried her idea out loud, low enough that only he could hear. "Take away three from both sides. The scale stays level. Then you have 2k equals twelve, so k equals six."

Marcus blinked at her notebook. "So the letter's just a kilometre?" He tried it on his own problem, subtracting from both sides, and his face opened up like a window. He grabbed her receipt before she could stop him. "Wait, is this the taxi thing you were muttering about at lunch? Do the same thing. Three plus 2k equals fifteen. Take away three, that's 2k equals twelve. Six kilometres. You went six kilometres." He grinned. "Give me that receipt for the contest, I'll write it up as my word problem. You already know the answer, so what do you need it for?"

Noemie snatched it back. She did need it, actually, and she told him so. She wanted to be the one to show her grandmother, tonight at the kitchen table, exactly how far they had travelled. She smoothed the paper flat, copying the equation beneath the printed numbers so it would look official. Somewhere in the city was a real road, six kilometres long, that she and Grandma had ridden down without once measuring it, and now she could prove it.

She looked up and found Mr. Okafor standing over her desk, reading her notebook. "Six kilometres," Noemie said, almost holding her breath. He picked up the receipt, studied it, and set it back down without a single word of explanation, which she decided was the best compliment she had gotten all year. Then he pointed at Marcus's paper and said, "Show me the one you stole."

activity: to describe their family and pets in a new language using full sentences
story:
Natalie had renamed the dog twice already in Spanish and both takes were ruined. The first time her little brother Theo walked through the frame eating a granola bar, and the second time she sneezed in the middle of "mi hermano tiene doce años." Now she was setting up the phone on a stack of cookbooks for take three, determined to get the whole video for Spanish class in one clean shot.

"Can you two be quiet for ninety seconds?" she asked. "I'm advocating here for a single take. One."

"You're not advocating," Theo said. "You're just asking louder than normal."

Peanut, the dog, thumped her tail against the floor from the doorway, hopeful, as always, that a stack of cookbooks meant food. Peanut was small and brown and female, which mattered in a way Natalie was about to find out.

The third take was going beautifully. "Mi madre es enfermera," Natalie said. "Mi padre trabaja en una oficina. Mi hermano es ruidoso." Theo made a face behind the phone but stayed silent. Then she pointed at the doorway and said, "Tengo un perro. Se llama Peanut. El perro es pequeño y simpático."

From the kitchen doorway, Abuela, who was visiting and had been quietly shredding chicken the whole time, looked up. "Peanut is a girl," she said. "La perra. A male dog is el perro, and a female dog is la perra."

Natalie stopped the recording. She stared at Peanut, who stared back with her ears up, completely unbothered. So the word for dog wasn't just one word. It changed depending on whether the dog was a boy or a girl, and nobody had mentioned that in class, where every example had been some generic dog with no name and no feelings about it.

She decided to test it before she trusted it. "Abuela, if Peanut were a boy, what would I say?"

"El perro," Abuela said, still shredding.

"And because she's a girl?"

"La perra."

Same dog, different word, depending on something you couldn't see just by looking at the vocabulary list. Natalie had assumed there was one right answer, the way there's one right answer for how to spell "restaurante." Apparently Spanish kept secrets.

"This is like the blender," their dad called from the kitchen. "The manual never tells you the important stuff until it's too late, and then it turns out the warranty doesn't cover it."

"The warranty on what?" Theo asked. "The dog?"

"Take four," Natalie announced, and pressed record. This time she said it slowly and carefully, pointing at Peanut like a game show host presenting a prize: "Tengo una perra. Se llama Peanut. La perra es pequeña y simpática." Peanut, hearing her name, trotted over and put one muddy paw directly on the lens.

"That was spontaneous," Theo said. "I liked it."

Natalie looked at the smudged, paw-printed footage, then at the dog, then at the stack of cookbooks. "Take five," she said, and went to get a paper towel.
